lesson.title: Who Owns the Electrons: An Introduction to Formal Charge
lesson.summary: Formal charge is a bookkeeping tool that assigns a hypothetical charge to each atom in a Lewis structure by assuming perfectly equal electron sharing, helping chemists judge which Lewis structure is most realistic.
lesson.body:
A Lewis structure can satisfy every octet and still not be the most realistic picture of a molecule if there is more than one way to connect the atoms or place the bonds. Formal charge is the tool chemists use to judge realism. It answers a simple hypothetical question for each atom: if every bonding pair were split perfectly evenly between the two atoms sharing it, ignoring real differences in electronegativity, what charge would this atom appear to have compared to its neutral, isolated state?

The formula is formal charge equals the atom's normal number of valence electrons, minus the number of electrons in its lone pairs, minus half the number of electrons in its bonding pairs. Lone pairs belong entirely to the atom that holds them, which is why they are subtracted in full, while bonding pairs are split evenly between two atoms, which is why only half of a bonding pair's electrons count toward each atom. It helps to remember that formal charge is not a molecule's actual, measurable charge, real charge distribution depends on electronegativity differences too, it is only a diagnostic device for comparing candidate Lewis structures against each other on equal footing.

Ammonia, NH3, is a good starting example because nitrogen's formal charge comes out to zero, matching the fact that ammonia is a neutral molecule. Nitrogen normally has 5 valence electrons. In NH3 it has one lone pair, 2 nonbonding electrons, and three bonding pairs, 6 electrons total in bonds, so 3 count toward nitrogen. Formal charge on nitrogen: 5 minus 2 minus 3 equals 0. Each hydrogen, with 1 valence electron, no lone pairs, and one bonding pair, 1 electron counted, gives 1 minus 0 minus 1 equals 0. Every atom checks out at zero, consistent with ammonia's overall neutral charge.

Now compare that to the ammonium ion, NH4+. Here nitrogen forms a fourth bond to a hydrogen ion and keeps no lone pair at all. Nitrogen now has zero lone pairs and four bonding pairs, 8 electrons in bonds, 4 counted toward nitrogen. Formal charge on nitrogen: 5 minus 0 minus 4 equals plus 1. Each hydrogen is still 1 minus 0 minus 1 equals 0. Adding up all five formal charges, plus 1 from nitrogen and 0 from each of the four hydrogens, gives plus 1 overall, matching the ion's actual charge. Losing that lone pair to form a new bond is exactly what shows up as the positive formal charge.

This rule, that the sum of all formal charges in a structure must equal the molecule's or ion's overall charge, is a built in error check for every Lewis structure you draw. It also becomes the deciding tool when a molecule has multiple plausible resonance structures or atom arrangements: the most realistic structure is generally the one with formal charges closest to zero, and where nonzero formal charges are unavoidable, negative formal charge is more reasonable on a more electronegative atom. The next section works through that decision process in full detail with a real example.
